history_of_present_illness: Pellagra is essentially a chronic disease with periodic exacerbations, though it may run a rather acute and rapidly fatal course. The typical symptom progression includes mild neurasthenic manifestations in winter (dizziness, insomnia, apprehension, occipital heaviness, muscular fatigue, mouth sensitivity, epigastric discomfort), followed in spring by disturbances of the alimentary tract (stomatitis, burning sensations up the esophagus, gastric eructations, pyrosis, and recurring diarrheas, or occasionally mild dysentery). The third and diagnostically most important group of symptoms are those of the cutaneous system: strikingly symmetrical, sharply delimited patches of erythema, resembling sunburn, appear on sun-exposed areas such as the backs of hands, forearms, bridge of nose, cheeks, forehead, neck, and sometimes scrotum, feet, or elbows. This erythema often persists, with desquamation lasting weeks or months, and striking pigmentation at the borders. Skin lesions can range from dry, scaly, and atrophic to moist and oedematous, potentially with bullae or gangrene. The neurasthenia tends to progress to more distinct neurological manifestations like variations in reflexes, tremors (especially of the tongue, head, and upper extremities), a depressed mental state, lack of mental concentration, or memory lapses. In advanced stages, a toxic psychosis or confusional insanity may develop, often characterized by mutism and melancholia. The final stage is marked by cachexia, dementia, loss of vesical sphincter control, and terminal diarrhea. Recurrences of clinical manifestations each spring are striking features, though they may skip a year. The disease is described in prodromal, first, second, and third (cachectic) stages, which refer to severity rather than a strict sequence. Prodromal symptoms, such as malaise, weight loss, strength loss, and vertigo, are non-specific. In the first stage, alimentary issues include fissured mouth angles, an indented tongue (initially coated centrally with bare glistening sides/tips, later bare, red, fissured), red buccal mucosa, increased saliva, and tender/swollen/bleeding gums. Gastric disturbances include gastralgia, pyrosis, and eructations. Nervous symptoms include vertigo, occipital headaches, depression, and insomnia. The second stage sees aggravation of skin and alimentary symptoms with pronounced neurological signs: tremors of tongue and hands, great muscular weakness of legs, various paraesthesias, pain on pressure in the dorsal and lumbar back, and an abnormal gait. The mental state becomes confused, depressed, and often morose, with simple retardation being common. The third stage is defined by confusional insanity and terminal cachexia. A severe form, 'typhoid pellagra', can present with high fever and symptoms resembling toxic typhoid, or acute delirium similar to paresis, often as a terminal event. Cases without skin lesions are termed 'pellagra sine pellagra'.
